families.name: Washing machines
families.summary: A washing machine is a sealed tub that fills, washes, empties and spins. Most “it’s broken” moments are one of those steps failing — not a mystery computer. This page is a reference you can read without starting a chat: what is usually going on, what you can safely look at, and what you should leave alone.
families.about: UK washing machine help: what a drain, leak, spin or door-lock problem usually means, which checks are safe at home, and when to stop and use the diagnostic assistant.

commonProblems.title: Won’t drain
commonProblems.detail: If the cycle sticks on empty, or there is standing water in the drum, the water cannot get out. On most UK machines that path is: drum → pump filter (behind a small flap at the bottom front) → drain pump → drain hose into a standpipe or sink waste. A blocked filter or a coin in the pump is common. Dirty water that comes back after a successful pump-out is often the household waste pipe, not the machine.

commonProblems.title: Won’t spin / clothes soaking
commonProblems.detail: Spin needs a locked door, an empty sump, and a drum that can accelerate. A machine that washed but will not spin may be detecting an out-of-balance load, a door that did not lock, or water still in the drum. Do not force the drum round by hand while it is powered.

commonProblems.title: Won’t fill
commonProblems.detail: No water in, or a trickle then an error, usually means the tap is off, a kinked fill hose, or the small mesh filter in the hose connector is blocked with grit. A failed inlet valve is possible, but check the hose and tap first.

commonProblems.title: Leaking
commonProblems.detail: Where the water appears matters. Damp around the door often points to the rubber door seal (the boot). A wet detergent drawer can be overdosing or a blocked drawer. A puddle from underneath during empty can be a loose drain hose, a cracked filter housing, or a failed pump seal. Unplug before you look underneath, and do not run another cycle into a flood.

commonProblems.title: Banging, walking or very noisy
commonProblems.detail: A new or recently moved machine that hammers on spin often still has transit bolts in the back — they hold the drum for delivery and must come out before use. An older machine that suddenly grinds or walks may have a lumpy load, unmet feet, or worn drum bearings (a repair, not a DIY strip-down).

commonProblems.title: Door will not lock or open
commonProblems.detail: The door lock (interlock) keeps the door shut during a wash. After a cycle, wait two or three minutes — many locks release on a delay. If the drum still has water, drain it first; the lock is designed not to open on a full tub. Do not lever the door.

commonProblems.title: Musty smell or drain smell
commonProblems.detail: A mouldy or “wet towel” smell usually lives in the door-seal fold and detergent drawer — wipe and rinse those. A sharp drain or sewer smell after emptying is more often the household trap or standpipe than the machine itself.

commonProblems.title: Error codes
commonProblems.detail: A code is a clue, not a parts list. The same letters mean different things on different brands. Photograph the display and describe what the machine was doing when it appeared — drain, spin, fill, or door — rather than searching the code on its own.

safeChecks.title: Pump filter (safe if you drain first)
safeChecks.detail: Switch the machine off at the wall. Open the bottom-front flap. Have a shallow tray and towel ready: a little water will come. Twist the filter out and pick out lint, coins and hair. Typical layout — yours may differ.

safeChecks.title: Fill-hose mesh
safeChecks.detail: Turn the tap off. Unscrew the hose from the tap end and rinse the small mesh that catches grit. Do not lose the washer in the coupling.

safeChecks.title: Door-seal fold and detergent drawer
safeChecks.detail: Peel back the lower fold of the rubber door seal and wipe it. Pull the detergent drawer right out and rinse residue. These are hygiene checks, not a drain repair.

safeChecks.title: Transit bolts and level feet
safeChecks.detail: From the back, check the large bolts that lock the drum for transport have been removed. Rock the machine gently: all four feet should sit firmly. A walking machine on spin is often unmet feet or leftover bolts, not a “broken drum”.

safetyNotes.title: Water and electricity together
safetyNotes.detail: Standing water around the plug, socket or flex: switch off at the consumer unit if you cannot reach a dry switch safely. Do not paddle while it is plugged in.

safetyNotes.title: Burning, smoke or sparks
safetyNotes.detail: Stop the machine, isolate power, and do not run another cycle. A hot-electrics smell is not the same as a first-use “new heater” smell — if you see smoke or scorch marks, stop.

safetyNotes.title: Repeated RCD or breaker trips
safetyNotes.detail: A machine that kills the RCD when it heats or fills should stay unplugged until diagnosed. That is not a “reset and hope” fault.

findingYourModel.detail: Open the door and look around the rim, or just inside the frame. Some brands put a second plate on the back. You need the model number (not just the marketing name on the front) before anyone can talk about a matching part.
tips: Wipe condensation off the sticker before photographing it.
Include the make, model and any serial line in the photo.
If the sticker has worn away, the manual or purchase email sometimes still has the model.

families.name: Washer dryers
families.summary: A washer dryer is one cabinet doing two jobs: a wash system (fill, wash, drain, spin) and a drying system (heat and airflow, often with a condenser and a fluff path). A fault that appears “on the dry” is not automatically the same as a standalone tumble dryer, and a wash leak is not a dry-heater problem. Treat the two halves separately when you describe what happened.
families.about: UK washer dryer help: washing problems, poor drying, condenser care, and when a combined machine needs an engineer rather than another mixed cycle.

commonProblems.title: Washes but will not dry
commonProblems.detail: If clothes come out washed and spun, the wash half did its job. Poor drying is then heat, airflow or condenser/water-tank related. Overloading a combo dryer is easy — the dry load limit is much smaller than the wash load. A machine that never gets warm on dry, with a clean filter, is a different story from one that is warm but still damp.

commonProblems.title: Drying half smells hot or cuts out
commonProblems.detail: Lint in a washer dryer’s dry path is a fire-risk housekeeping issue. Clean the fluff filter every dry cycle if it has one, and do not ignore a burning-dust smell. If it trips the supply on dry only, stop using the dry programme.

commonProblems.title: Not draining on the wash
commonProblems.detail: The wash drain path is still a pump filter and hose, as on a washing machine. A combo unit can also leave extra water because a dry cycle expected a spun load. Standing water after wash is a drain problem first, not a dryer element.

commonProblems.title: Leaking during wash or dry
commonProblems.detail: Wash leaks (door, drawer, pump) are the same family as a washer. A leak only on dry can be condenser water that has nowhere to go — a full tank, a blocked condenser drain, or a cracked tank hose inside. Unplug before opening lower panels.

commonProblems.title: Takes forever or never finishes a combo cycle
commonProblems.detail: Combined programmes that wash then dry will abort or loop if spin failed, the load is huge, or the dryer cannot reach a target dryness. Note whether it stalled on wash, spin, or dry — that split is the useful fact.

commonProblems.title: Door locked after a dry
commonProblems.detail: The lock still follows water and temperature rules. A hot drum or remaining water can keep it shut. Wait it out; do not force it. If it stays locked when cold and empty, describe that as a lock fault, not a dry fault.

safeChecks.title: Dry load size
safeChecks.detail: If you washed a full drum then pressed Dry, the machine is overloaded for drying. Take half the clothes out and try dry only. This is the most useful combo-specific check and costs nothing.

safeChecks.title: Fluff filter and condenser path
safeChecks.detail: Where the machine has a fluff filter in the door or bellows, clean it every dry. Condenser washer dryers also need the condenser and water container emptied or cleaned — a full tank stops drying and can leak.

safeChecks.title: Wash pump filter
safeChecks.detail: If the wash will not empty, use the same bottom-front filter check as a washing machine: isolate power, catch the water, twist the filter out.

safetyNotes.title: Burning smell on dry
safetyNotes.detail: Stop the dry programme, unplug, and do not run dry again until the fluff path is cleared or the machine is diagnosed. Lint plus heat is how laundry fires start.

safetyNotes.title: Supply trips only on dry
safetyNotes.detail: A heater or fan that trips the RCD is an electrical fault. Leave dry unused. Wash-only may still be unsafe if the same supply circuit is involved — if in doubt, isolate the appliance.

safetyNotes.title: Water around the socket
safetyNotes.detail: Same rule as any laundry machine: isolate power from a dry place. Do not open the back while it is wet and live.

findingYourModel.detail: Look on the door rim when the door is open, or on the rear panel. Washer dryer model numbers are specific — a “same looking” washer without dry is a different model. Photograph the whole sticker.
tips: Note the rated wash load and dry load if printed; they are often different.
If you only use wash, still tell the assistant it is a washer dryer so the dry half is not invented.

families.name: Tumble dryers
families.summary: A tumble dryer tumbles clothes through warm air, then gets rid of the moisture — either by venting it outside or by condensing it into a tank. Almost every “not drying” complaint starts with airflow. Heaters fail too, but a clogged fluff filter or condenser is the check that actually belongs to you.
families.about: UK tumble dryer help: lint filters, condensers, dryers that run but do not heat, and when overheating means stop using it.

commonProblems.title: Runs but clothes stay wet
commonProblems.detail: If the drum turns, the motor is doing something. Wet clothes then usually mean no useful heat or no useful airflow. Clean the filter, condenser (if it has one) and vents before assuming a heater or thermostat has failed.

commonProblems.title: Drum turns but there is no warmth
commonProblems.detail: Reach in mid-cycle, carefully: if the drum spins but the air is cold, the heat side has stopped while the motor runs on. On vented and older condenser models that is often a thermal cut-out tripped by a blocked filter or vent — clear the airflow first, because a new heater fitted behind a blocked filter just trips again. Heat-pump models dry cool by design, so “not very warm” is normal for them; judge those on dryness and time, not on heat.

commonProblems.title: Takes too long / poor drying
commonProblems.detail: Restricted airflow makes the machine work longer and run hotter. Overloading has the same effect. Heat-pump dryers especially hate a dirty filter — they dry cool and slowly when neglected, then error.

commonProblems.title: Tank full / condenser wet mess
commonProblems.detail: Condenser and heat-pump models collect water. If the tank is full every twenty minutes, or water appears at the bottom door, the pump-out path or condenser is blocked — or the tank is not seated.

commonProblems.title: Stops partway through the cycle
commonProblems.detail: A dryer that pauses or ends early is not always broken. A full water tank halts condenser and heat-pump models until you empty it; a door not quite latched, an anti-crease hold at the end of the programme, or a moisture sensor reading the load as dry can all look like a mid-cycle stop. If it stops and the cabinet is hot, treat it as overheating (below) rather than pressing start again.

commonProblems.title: Too hot, scorching or cutting out
commonProblems.detail: Overheating is a stop-using-it moment if you smell scorching, see browning on clothes, or the machine trips. That is airflow or a safety thermostat doing its last job. Let it cool. Do not bypass thermal cut-outs.

commonProblems.title: Noisy drum or will not tumble
commonProblems.detail: Rattles can be a zip in the drum — empty it and look. A grinding drum with no clothes in it is bearings or rollers, which is a repair. Do not run a dryer that smells of hot rubber belt until it is checked.

safeChecks.title: Lint / fluff filter every load
safeChecks.detail: Lift the filter from the door opening or rim, peel the fluff off, and slot it back fully. A half-seated filter can blow lint into the machine.

safeChecks.title: Condenser and water tank
safeChecks.detail: On condenser dryers the tank pulls out at the top; the condenser slides out behind a lower front flap. Rinse fluff off the condenser until the water runs clear. Switch off and let it cool first.

safeChecks.title: Vents and the room
safeChecks.detail: Vented dryers need an unobstructed hose to outside — not a crushed pipe behind the machine. All dryers need space around the back. A bone-dry cupboard with no air is a poor place to dry laundry.

safetyNotes.title: Scorching, smoke or a lint fire
safetyNotes.detail: Unplug if you can do it safely, get people out if there is smoke, and do not open a roaring dryer to “see”. Lint fires are real.

safetyNotes.title: Breaker trips when it heats
safetyNotes.detail: Leave it isolated. That is not a filter problem.

safetyNotes.title: Cabinet too hot to touch
safetyNotes.detail: Stop using it. Overheat cut-outs exist because dryers start fires when airflow is gone.

findingYourModel.detail: Look around the door opening, just inside, or on a rear/side plate. Note whether it is vented, condenser or heat pump if the sticker says so — drying advice changes.
tips: Photograph the model before you pull the machine out; rear plates are easy to miss in poor light.
Vented dryers have a hose or outlet at the back; condenser and heat-pump models have a pull-out water tank near the top — knowing which you have changes the advice.

families.name: Dishwashers
families.summary: A dishwasher is a heated, circulating wash with a drain pump and a filter that is meant to be cleaned. Cloudy glasses, wet plastic on the top rack, or a puddle on the floor each point at different parts of that loop. None of them are fixed by pouring more rinse aid into a blocked filter.
families.about: UK dishwasher help: cloudy glasses, standing water, spray arms, filters, and when a leak or electrical trip means stop using it.

commonProblems.title: Standing water / will not drain
commonProblems.detail: Water left over the heating element or sloshing in the base is a drain-path problem: filter, pump, or drain hose (including a high loop or sink waste that is backing up). Run a drain-only or cancel, then check the filter before calling it a dead pump.

commonProblems.title: Poor cleaning or gritty crockery
commonProblems.detail: If the spray arms cannot spin or the jets are blocked with food, nothing else in the chemistry will save the wash. Overloading, a clogged filter, and a dead wash pump all look similar until you spin the arms by hand (machine off).

commonProblems.title: White film or cloudy glasses
commonProblems.detail: Hard water, too much detergent in a soft-water area, or rinse aid empty can all haze glass. That is not the same as a heater that never gets the water hot — greasy soil left on plates is a heat or wash-pump clue, not a rinse-aid clue.

commonProblems.title: Leaking from the door
commonProblems.detail: Foam from the wrong detergent (washing-up liquid is a classic) overflows the door. A torn door seal, a blocked salt cap, or a machine that is not level can also weep. Wipe the foam, don’t keep restarting into suds.

commonProblems.title: Will not fill or keeps stopping
commonProblems.detail: Inlet hoses have a flood-stop jacket on many UK installs — if that bladder has tripped, the hose is designed to refuse water. Check the tap under the sink and whether the hose feels swollen.

commonProblems.title: Smells stale
commonProblems.detail: Food in the filter and a stagnant sump smell like a drain. Clean the filter, run a hot empty cycle with dishwasher cleaner if you use it, and do not store wet dishes in a sealed machine for days.

safeChecks.title: Twist-out filter
safeChecks.detail: Remove the bottom basket. The cylindrical filter usually twists anticlockwise from the floor of the tub. Rinse it under the tap. If the mesh is torn, it will not strain food — that is a part, not a rinse.

safeChecks.title: Spray arms
safeChecks.detail: Check the lower (and upper) arm spins freely and the jet holes are not plugged with seeds or grit. Most arms unclip or unscrew at the centre. Rinse them; do not poke metal into ceramic jets.

safeChecks.title: Salt, rinse aid, and the right detergent
safeChecks.detail: If you have a water softener, keep salt filled and the cap tight — a loose cap dumps salt water into the tub and corrodes steel. Rinse aid helps glass. Never use washing-up liquid.

safetyNotes.title: Water on the kitchen floor near sockets
safetyNotes.detail: Isolate power. Under-sink sockets and a leaking inlet hose are a bad mix.

safetyNotes.title: RCD trips mid-cycle
safetyNotes.detail: Often the heater. Do not keep resetting to “just finish the plates”.

safetyNotes.title: Burning or melted plastic smell
safetyNotes.detail: Stop. A utensil on the element or a failing heater can scorch. Let it cool before you look.

findingYourModel.detail: Open the door and look on the side or top edge of the door, or on a sticker on the tub wall. Rear plates exist but are awkward behind kitchen plinths.
tips: Photograph the door-edge sticker before the kitchen fitter’s plinth goes back on.
The FD or product number is more useful than the retail “model name” on the front.

families.name: Fridge-freezers
families.summary: A fridge-freezer moves heat out of the cabinet with a sealed refrigeration circuit, fans, and a control that decides when the compressor runs. You can check doors, vents and dirt on the condenser. You cannot add gas, “recharge” it from a can, or puncture pipework — that work is for a qualified engineer and is regulated.
families.about: UK fridge-freezer help: when food is not cold enough, ice build-up, noisy compressors, and why sealed-system gas is never a DIY top-up.

commonProblems.title: Fridge warm, freezer okay — or the reverse
commonProblems.detail: Different compartments have different airflow. A blocked internal vent, a failed flap, or a fan that has iced solid can warm one side while the other still feels fine. Note which compartment failed and whether the back wall is iced over.

commonProblems.title: Everything warm, compressor silent or clicking
commonProblems.detail: If you hear no compressor after several minutes, or it clicks every few seconds and gives up, that is not a “turn the dial up” problem. Keep the doors shut to save the food you have, and describe the sound.

commonProblems.title: Ice city / water on the floor
commonProblems.detail: Auto-defrost models drain melt water to a tray above the compressor. If that drain holes ices up, water appears in the fridge or on the floor. Never chip ice with a knife — you can puncture the evaporator.

commonProblems.title: Noisy, rattling or vibrating
commonProblems.detail: A fridge should hum. A scream, knock, or rattle that started after you pulled it out to clean may just be a pipe touching the cabinet — but a dying fan or compressor has a different, constant pitch. Say when it makes the noise (during cooling, or all the time).

commonProblems.title: Food freezing in the fridge
commonProblems.detail: Over-cooling can be a thermostat, a damper stuck open to the freezer, or food sat against the back plate. It is the opposite of “not cooling” and needs that distinction in any diagnosis.

safeChecks.title: Door seal and loading
safeChecks.detail: Close the door on a piece of paper: it should drag. Dirty or torn seals leak warm air and make ice. Do not pack the fridge so tight that internal vents are blocked.

safeChecks.title: Space and condenser dust
safeChecks.detail: Most UK freestanding models dump heat through coils or a rear panel. Pull the machine out (carefully, with help), unplug it, and vacuum dust from the back and the floor underneath. Leave a gap as the manufacturer specified — usually a few centimetres.

safeChecks.title: Temperature setting
safeChecks.detail: Aim around 4 °C in the fridge and −18 °C in the freezer if you have a display. A holiday setting or a child-lock can look like a fault.

safetyNotes.title: Do not puncture or “regas”
safetyNotes.detail: Refrigerant circuit work is not a consumer job. Cans sold online are not a fix for a leaking system, and damaging the pipework writes the appliance off.

safetyNotes.title: Electrical burning or trips
safetyNotes.detail: Unplug. A fridge that trips the supply can be the compressor or defrost heater.

safetyNotes.title: You cannot keep food safe
safetyNotes.detail: If temperatures have been in the danger zone for hours, the food safety decision is yours — diagnosis will not make yesterday’s chicken safe.

findingYourModel.detail: Look inside the fridge — side wall, beside the salad drawers, or behind a kick plate. Some plates are on the rear. You want the model, not the litre capacity printed on the sales badge.
tips: Take the photo with the door open in good light; condensation hides digits.
If you have an American-style double door, check both liners.

families.name: Ovens and cookers
families.summary: An oven is a box that must get hot evenly and stay sealed. Electric models use elements, a fan (on fan ovens), and a thermostat. Gas models add burners and a flame-supervision device. If you smell gas, this page does not ask you to diagnose anything — you leave, you ventilate, you call the emergency number.
families.about: UK oven and cooker help: uneven baking, no heat, fan ovens, and what to do if you smell gas. Not a Gas Safe visit and not a DIY wiring guide.

commonProblems.title: Not heating, or only the grill works
commonProblems.detail: A fan oven with a dead hidden element can still blow cold air. A grill that works while the oven does not often means a different element or a selector switch — useful to say up front. For gas, no click and no smell of gas at the burner is different from smell of gas.

commonProblems.title: Uneven cooking or one side pale
commonProblems.detail: Fan, element, temperature sensor and door seal all take a share. A dropped door that no longer sits square leaks heat at the corners. This is identification first; swapping elements is an engineer job on a built-in, often hard-wired cooker.

commonProblems.title: Fan noisy or not spinning
commonProblems.detail: A shriek from the back of a fan oven is often the fan motor. Do not run a fan oven for hours with a seized fan: food will not cook evenly and the element can overheat locally.

commonProblems.title: Door, glass or hinge
commonProblems.detail: A door that drops, a cracked inner glass, or a lock on a pyrolytic cycle that will not release are mechanical faults. Pyrolytic locks stay shut while the cavity is dangerously hot — wait for cool-down; do not force them.

commonProblems.title: Clock, timer or it will not start
commonProblems.detail: Many ovens refuse to heat if the clock is unset after a power cut. That is not an element failure. If the display is dead on a hard-wired cooker, isolate at the wall switch and treat it as electrical.

safeChecks.title: Power and the wall switch
safeChecks.detail: Built-in ovens are often on a switched fused connection above a cupboard. Confirm that switch is on before assuming a dead element. Do not open the terminal block.

safeChecks.title: Door seal and shelves
safeChecks.detail: A flattened or torn seal wastes heat. Shelves blocking the fan outlet in a fan oven give pale centres. These are observations, not wiring tests.

safeChecks.title: Gas: if cold, check the obvious only
safeChecks.detail: If a gas oven does not light, you may look whether the cooker isolation valve is open — that is a handle, not a joint. If you smell gas, skip every check and follow the stop steps below.

safetyNotes.title: Smell of gas, faint hiss, or suspected leak
safetyNotes.detail: Do not use electrical switches, including the doorbell. Open windows, get out if the smell is strong, and call the Gas Emergency Services on 0800 111 999. Do not “find the leak” with a flame or by tightening joints.

safetyNotes.title: Carbon monoxide concerns
safetyNotes.detail: Headache, nausea, sooty yellow gas flames that will not sit on the burner: stop using the appliance, ventilate, get fresh air, and seek medical advice if you feel unwell. Have gas appliances inspected by a Gas Safe engineer.

safetyNotes.title: Sparks, burning, or a tripped cooker circuit
safetyNotes.detail: Leave it isolated. Cooker circuits are high current. Terminal-block burns on the back of a cooker are an engineer job, not a customer reseat.

safetyNotes.title: Hot surfaces and pyrolytic
safetyNotes.detail: Do not reach into a pyrolytic cycle. Do not put tea towels on a hot hob above a cooker oven.

findingYourModel.detail: Look around the door frame, behind a storage drawer, or on the rear (you may need to ease the cooker out with the supply isolated). Built-in ovens often have the plate on the frame once the door is open.
tips: Note whether it is gas, electric, or dual fuel before you start a diagnosis.
A first-fix cooker switch being off is embarrassingly common — check it.

families.name: Hobs
families.summary: A hob is only the cooking surface: gas burners, ceramic radiant zones, or induction coils under glass. It is not the oven underneath (if you have a separate cooker, use the oven page for the cavity). The useful question is which zone failed, whether it clicks, and whether the glass is intact.
families.about: UK hob help: rings that will not heat, ignition click, induction cookware, cracked ceramic glass, and gas-smell boundaries.

commonProblems.title: One zone dead, others fine
commonProblems.detail: That pattern usually belongs to one burner, one radiant element, or one induction coil/inverter — not the whole mains. Say which zone (front left, etc.) and whether it is gas, ceramic or induction.

commonProblems.title: Whole hob dead — no zones, no display
commonProblems.detail: When nothing lights and no zone heats, think supply before board. Many hobs sit on their own fused spur or a cooker switch that is easy to knock off; a tripped RCD or a blown fuse in the spur kills the lot. After a power cut, some hobs will not respond until the clock is set or a child lock is cleared. A hob that stays completely dead with a confirmed live supply is a control-board or internal fault — not something you reset from the top of the glass.

commonProblems.title: A zone cuts in and out while cooking
commonProblems.detail: Induction zones share power and protect themselves from heat: a big pan on boost can make a neighbouring zone drop power, and a zone sat over a hot inverter will throttle or pause until it cools. That is designed behaviour, not a fault. A zone that flickers on any pan, buzzes in a new way, or cuts with a repeated gap can instead be a loose connection or a tiring coil — note whether it is one zone only or the whole hob.

commonProblems.title: Induction will not detect a pan
commonProblems.detail: The pan must be ferrous and roughly the size of the zone. A small pan on a large zone, or aluminium/copper without a steel base, looks like a broken hob. Try a magnet on the pan base. If a known-good pan fails on every zone, that is the hob.

commonProblems.title: Gas clicks but will not light
commonProblems.detail: Ignition can click while the gas valve is closed, a jet is blocked with overboil, or the burner cap is sat crooked. If you smell gas while it is clicking, stop — that is not a “keep clicking” situation.

commonProblems.title: Error or fault code on the display
commonProblems.detail: Induction and ceramic hobs flash codes like F, E or a symbol for overheating, a pan problem, or a sensor fault. The same letter means different things on different brands, so photograph the display and note what you were doing — boost on one zone, an empty pan left on, or a spill across the controls. An “L” or padlock symbol is a child lock, not a breakdown.

commonProblems.title: Cracked ceramic or induction glass
commonProblems.detail: A cracked hob top is a stop-using-it fault. Liquids can reach live parts. Do not “make do” with foil over the crack.

commonProblems.title: Touch controls dead or locked
commonProblems.detail: A child lock, a wet control panel, or a power cut that left the hob in lock can look like a total failure. Dry the glass and look for an ‘L’ or key symbol before assuming a control board.

safeChecks.title: Cookware (induction)
safeChecks.detail: Magnet sticks to the base: probably suitable. Very warped bases sit badly. This check avoids a false “hob is dead” on a new pan.

safeChecks.title: Burner caps sat flat (gas)
safeChecks.detail: When the hob is cold, lift the pan support and check the cap is centred. Overboil debris in the spark ignitor can be brushed off gently — machine off, no solvents in the jet.

safeChecks.title: Isolation switch
safeChecks.detail: Many hobs have a fused spur nearby. Confirm it is on. Do not open the spur.

safeChecks.title: Clear a lock or a power-cut sulk
safeChecks.detail: If the controls look dead, dry the glass fully, then hold the lock or key button for a few seconds to clear a child lock. After a power cut some hobs need the time set before any zone will fire. These cost nothing and rule out a false “dead board”.

safetyNotes.title: Gas smell
safetyNotes.detail: Same as cookers: no switches, ventilate, out if strong, 0800 111 999. Do not keep sparking a burner that is flooding gas.

safetyNotes.title: Cracked glass
safetyNotes.detail: Switch off at the isolation point. Do not cook on a cracked ceramic or induction surface.

safetyNotes.title: Burning under the glass or trips
safetyNotes.detail: Isolate. Residual heat warnings can stay on after a fault — still treat trips as electrical, not as a pan problem.

findingYourModel.detail: Often on the underside of the hob (you would only see it when the hob is out) or on the original paperwork. Some have a line on the rim under a pan stand. If you cannot see it without lifting a built-in hob, do not lift it — describe the brand from the glass and photograph any visible strip.
tips: Never lever a sealed hob out to read a sticker; that is how you crack the worktop or the glass.
A photo of the control panel plus brand is still useful if the plate is inaccessible.

families.name: Microwaves
families.summary: A microwave cooks with high-voltage energy inside a shielded box. The door, the mesh in the glass, and the seals are part of that shield. If the motor turns the plate but food stays cold, that is a heating-chain fault — and the dangerous parts of that chain are not customer-accessible. This page will not tell you how to open the cabinet, test a magnetron, or discharge a capacitor. Those parts hold a lethal charge even after unplugging.
families.about: UK microwave help: when the turntable turns but food stays cold, sparking in the cavity, and why the cover must never come off.

commonProblems.title: Turns, lights, but food stays cold
commonProblems.detail: If the lamp and turntable work, the low-voltage side is doing something. No heat then sits in the high-voltage chain (magnetron and related parts) or in a door switch that lies about the door being shut. Either way, the next step is not a screwdriver to the cover.

commonProblems.title: Sparking or arcing in the cavity
commonProblems.detail: Stop using it. Sparks can come from metal, gold-rimmed china, a fork left in, a damaged waveguide cover (the mica sheet on the side wall), or a failing component. Remove obvious metal. If it still arcs on a microwave-safe bowl of water, stop — the cavity is not safe to keep using.

commonProblems.title: Door, latch or it will not start
commonProblems.detail: Several door switches must agree the door is closed. A door that drops, a broken latch, or a microwave that runs with the door questionable is a stop-using-it fault. Never bypass a door switch.

commonProblems.title: Turntable not turning
commonProblems.detail: The coupler under the glass plate can split, or the motor can fail. A plate that sits still still heats — but food will cook in hot spots. Check the roller ring is the right way up before assuming a motor.

commonProblems.title: Display dead, clock blank, or buttons do nothing
commonProblems.detail: A blank display with no fan and no light is usually supply: try the socket with something else, and check the plug fuse. A lit display that refuses to start can be a child lock (often a hold-to-clear button) or a demo or showroom mode left on after a power cut. A keypad where only some buttons respond points at the touch panel. None of this calls for the case to come off.

commonProblems.title: Cuts out, noisy, or smells of burning
commonProblems.detail: A loud buzz that is new, a burning smell, or a trip at the socket: unplug. Do not run “just 30 seconds more” to finish a meal.

safeChecks.title: A bowl of water, nothing else
safeChecks.detail: Place a microwave-safe bowl of water in the centre, no metal, and run a short time. If the water does not heat at all, you have a no-heat fault. If it heats, the appliance is producing energy — look at cookware and time. Stop if you see sparks.

safeChecks.title: Cavity and waveguide cover
safeChecks.detail: With it unplugged and cool, look for a burnt or missing sheet on the side wall (waveguide cover) and for food carbon. You can wipe the cavity. You cannot replace HV parts from this page.

safeChecks.title: Door mesh and seal
safeChecks.detail: The metal mesh in the door is not decorative. If the glass is broken or the mesh is damaged, do not use the microwave.

safetyNotes.title: Never remove the cover
safetyNotes.detail: High-voltage capacitors can hold a charge after the plug is out. There is no safe consumer test of a magnetron. If a video tells you otherwise, ignore it.

safetyNotes.title: Do not use it with a damaged door
safetyNotes.detail: A microwave that runs with the door open, or with a broken hinge, is not a bargain to keep using.

safetyNotes.title: Persistent arcing
safetyNotes.detail: Stop. Continued arcing damages the cavity and is a fire risk.

findingYourModel.detail: Look just inside the door opening or on a rear plate. You want the model, not only the wattage printed on the front.
tips: Wattage on the fascia is not a model number.
If you have a built-in microwave, the plate may be on the frame once the door is open.

families.name: Vacuum cleaners
families.summary: A vacuum is a fan (the motor) pulling air through a hose, filters, and a bag or bin. Loss of suction is almost always a full bin, a choked filter, or a blockage in the wand — not a “dead motor” — until those are cleared. Cordless models add a battery that can look like a motor fault when it is just empty or tired.
families.about: UK vacuum cleaner help: loss of suction, overheating cut-outs, brush bars that will not spin, and when a motor smell means stop.

commonProblems.title: Weak suction
commonProblems.detail: Work from the head back: clogged floor tool, blocked wand (a sock or Lego is a classic), full bag or bin, and filters packed with dust. A machine that sucks strongly at the hose inlet but not at the head has a blockage in the tools, not a new motor.

commonProblems.title: Suction pulses or surges in waves
commonProblems.detail: Pulsing — suction that throbs or revs up and down — is almost always an airflow problem, whatever the make. A near-blocked filter, a full bin, or a partial clog in the wand or head starves the motor of air, so it hunts and surges. Work the airflow path first: empty the bin, clean or dry the filters, and clear the hose and floor head. Only if the airflow is genuinely clear and a cordless model still pulses with a short runtime is the battery worth a look — pulsing on its own is not a battery verdict.

commonProblems.title: Cuts out after a minute
commonProblems.detail: Many motors have a thermal cut-out. A blocked machine runs hot and stops, then works again when cool. That is a blockage reminder, not a random electrical ghost. If it cuts out with a clean path, stop using it.

commonProblems.title: Brush bar will not spin
commonProblems.detail: Hair around the roller, a belt (on some uprights), or a clutch that disengages on a stuck bar. Cut hair out with scissors, unplugged. Do not keep running a jammed brush motor.

commonProblems.title: Will not turn on (mains or cordless)
commonProblems.detail: Mains: check the socket with a lamp. Cordless: charge status and a flashing battery mean power, not floorhead. A completely dead cordless after a drop can be a battery pack or a broken switch — still not something to prize open if the pack is swollen.

commonProblems.title: Cordless will not charge or dies in minutes
commonProblems.detail: Check the power path before the pack. Confirm the charger plug, the socket, and the charging light on the dock or tool: no light at all usually means the charger or its lead, not the battery. If it charges fully but then runs for only a couple of minutes, the pack is worn — a wear item on any make, replaced as a battery, not a sign the motor or head has failed. Do not keep charging a pack that is hot, swollen or smells.

commonProblems.title: Burning smell or smoke from the motor
commonProblems.detail: Unplug / isolate. A dust-packed motor or a dying armature smells of hot electrics. Do not “just finish the stairs”.

safeChecks.title: Bin or bag, then filters
safeChecks.detail: Empty the bin or replace the bag before anything clever. Wash only filters that the maker says are washable — some HEPA filters are dry-clean only and die if soaked. Dry washable filters fully before refitting or you will cook them.

safeChecks.title: Hose and wand
safeChecks.detail: Drop a coin or look through the wand. Flexible hoses crush internally; a hose that looks open can still be blocked inside the corrugations.

safeChecks.title: Head and brush
safeChecks.detail: Unplug. Cut hair off the roller. Check the suction inlet in the head is not taped over with a rug fringe.

safetyNotes.title: Swollen or leaking battery (cordless)
safetyNotes.detail: Do not charge it. Do not put it in household rubbish. Follow local battery disposal. A puffed pack is not a “keep using until it dies” part.

safetyNotes.title: Sparks from the motor bay or a trip
safetyNotes.detail: Stop. That is not a filter.

safetyNotes.title: Used on wet (unless it is a wet vac)
safetyNotes.detail: A dry vacuum that has sucked water is an electrical risk. Do not switch it back on to “dry it out”.

findingYourModel.detail: Look on the underside of the head, on the motor housing, or near where the hose enters the cylinder. Cordless sticks often hide the model in the battery well or on the wand.
tips: Upright and cylinder plates are easy to get dusty — wipe before the photo.
Battery voltage on a pack is not the vacuum model number.
